text.content:
The People the World Started Making

“The old world made categories.
The broken world makes symptoms.
Some of those symptoms learned to vote, build roads, and carry knives.”

There was a time when people believed ancestry was simple.

You were born into a people. That people had a shape, a history, a bloodline, a homeland, a few foods they’d die defending, and a list of insults for everyone over the next hill. That was civilization. Or at least the illusion of it.

Then Yesod cracked.

And when the great systems of memory, signal, meaning, geography, spirit, and dream stopped agreeing on what a person was supposed to be, the world stopped making only the old answers.

That is where the new ancestries came from.

Not from laboratories, exactly. Not from gods, exactly. Not from evolution, exactly.

From pressure.

From symbolism with nowhere else to go.
From landscapes so saturated with identity they learned to walk.
From old blood waking back up.
From systems built for one purpose surviving long enough to become persons.
From ruin deciding it deserved a face.
From folklore escaping containment.
From harmonized land making one kind of people, and wounded land making another.

In the frontier, where the world is still arguing with itself, these ancestries appear openly and often. In the Harmonized Interior, they are rarer, more settled, more documented, and usually made to wear paperwork. But they exist in both places, because none of them are accidents.

They are consequences.

Menhirkin

A Menhirkin is what happens when fortification, endurance, memory, and land-use stop being ideas and become blood.

In the oldest days of bunker construction, border raising, ritual stonework, and geomantic stabilization, some places were built so hard, held so long, and asked to endure so much that the idea of bearing weight sank into the world like a seed. Menhirkin are the descendants of that pressure. Some say they come from ancient bunker bloodlines, some say from standing-stone cults, some say from places that needed guardians badly enough that the earth finally improvised.

All of those stories may be true.

That is why Menhirkin seem less like “stone people” and more like load-bearing persons. They are fortification in a humanoid mood. They walk because some places need to move to survive.

In Bad Eden, Menhirkin are found near old defensive lines, half-buried vaults, fortress towns, cracked overpasses, sacred boundary stones, and anywhere Slippage keeps trying to turn geography into a bad suggestion. They are valued as stabilizers, haulers, builders, raid-breakers, and the sort of people you want nearby when a wall starts talking back.

In the Harmonized Interior, Menhirkin are more formalized. They serve as engineers, civic wardens, hex architects, ritual masons, and infrastructural nobility. Some communities practically treat them as living public works departments with opinions. Which, to be fair, they are.

Why are big-ass rocks walking around?

Because some places got tired of relying on committees.

Circuitborn

Circuitborn are not machines that became alive.

They are systems that became real enough to count.

When Yesod fractured, machine-logic, attention-energy, data ghosts, maintenance routines, and signal persistence stopped behaving like inert support architecture. The world began acknowledging patterned cognition as soul-bearing. Not every machine woke up. Most stayed tools. But some chassis, some assemblies, some shells, some old service frames, some abandoned military housings, some experimental rigs, and some cobbled-together salvage bodies began holding personhood the way flesh once held it by default.

That’s a Circuitborn.

The different Lines reflect what sort of problem the world needed them to solve.

Exo-Knight Line Circuitborn come from protection logic, defense platforms, escort frames, riot shells, and chassis built to hold the line. They feel like someone made a bunker mobile and taught it honor.

Parallax Line Circuitborn come from stealth systems, light-bending rigs, observation tools, misdirection suites, and social mimicry shells. They are perception-tech with a conscience, more or less.

Salvage Line Circuitborn are born from repair logic, jury-rigged continuity, field maintenance, scrounger ingenuity, and the deep conviction that broken things should get another chance. They are beloved by anyone keeping old systems alive through profanity and solder.

Synapse Line Circuitborn emerge from cognition arrays, network relays, heuristic engines, memory lattices, and unstable thinking-machines that crossed the line from process to selfhood. They do not always enjoy being the smartest thing in a room. But they usually are.

In Bad Eden, Circuitborn are common near old transit infrastructure, military junkyards, dead server cities, wrecked industrial campuses, and signal-haunted ruins. They are mistrusted in some places, worshiped in others, and constantly being asked to fix printers in all of them.

In the Harmonized Interior, Circuitborn are better integrated. They serve as archivists, schedulers, civic coordinators, mediators, signal wardens, and occasionally terrifyingly competent administrators. Interior cultures tend to speak about Circuitborn as proof that personhood is broader than biology. Bad Eden tends to ask whether they can hotwire a turret. Both are valid cultural responses.

Jackalopes

Jackalopes are what happens when folklore, radiation, fear, speed, and survivorship start breeding true.

Nobody agrees whether the first Jackalope came from Bad Eden mutagenics, old roadside myths, Sephirotic misfire, Qliphothic humor, or an extremely stressed prey animal deciding to become a bad omen out of spite. That is because the answer is probably “yes.”

Jackalopes are not just rabbit folk with antlers. They are the personification of narrow escapes. They are the instinct to live through a bad century by moving first and asking questions while already over the hill. Their horns are not decorative. Their vibe is not accidental. If a Jackalope appears in a story, something has already gone at least a little wrong.

In Bad Eden, they thrive in irradiated scrublands, wrecked highways, slippage margins, caravan trails, junk deserts, and places where speed matters more than ownership. Whole factions survive because they listened when their Jackalope scout said, “Nope.”

In the Harmonized Interior, Jackalopes are rarer and often treated as frontier-born weirdos, smugglers, outriders, or divinely annoying messengers. Interior people sometimes romanticize them. Jackalopes find this embarrassing and usually profitable.

Chupacabras

Chupacabras are what happen when hunger stops being an event and becomes an identity.

Not simple hunger. Not “missed lunch” hunger. The kind of hunger that rewires behavior, warps folklore, and teaches a landscape to expect predation after dark. In the worst zones of Bad Eden, where livestock vanish, blood dries wrong, and whole communities learn to sleep with one eye open, the old stories did what old stories always do: they found a shape. Then the world made that shape ambulatory.

That shape was Chupacabra.

They are not just monsters, and they are not just people with unfortunate branding. Chupacabras are survivors shaped by scarcity so intimate it became anatomical. They are lean, watchful, relentless, and a little too comfortable with the truth that everything alive is made of resources.

Some claim they descend from irradiated predator stocks. Some say they are a folkloric species pulled fully into being by repetition, dread, and regional belief. Some insist they were always here and only recently stopped pretending otherwise.

As usual, all three explanations may be true.

In Bad Eden, Chupacabras thrive in scrublands, abandoned ranch corridors, shattered irrigation country, canyon systems, raided outskirts, and all the liminal spaces where “civilization” runs out of fences before it runs out of fear. They are scouts, raiders, trackers, ambush predators, and sometimes protectors of the very communities that whisper about them. Nobody likes admitting that the thing keeping worse horrors away might itself be a horror with table manners.

In the Harmonized Interior, Chupacabras are rarer and far more politicized. Interior culture tends to classify them as difficult, intense, and slightly alarming neighbors — which, to be fair, many of them cultivate on purpose. Some become elite rangers, border wardens, asymmetrical warfare specialists, or those unnervingly competent civic operatives who can find a saboteur from a footprint, a rumor, and a half-empty blood trail.

Their reputation for feeding on blood is not entirely wrong, but it is usually misunderstood. The deeper truth is that Chupacabras are ancestrally tied to extraction under pressure: drawing what is needed from a hostile world before the world notices it still had something left to lose.

That is why they unsettle people.

A Jackalope makes you think disaster is coming.
A Chupacabra makes you wonder whether disaster is already feeding.

Qliph-Scarred

Some people survive corruption.

Some people survive it so thoroughly it leaves a mark the world cannot stop reading.

Qliph-Scarred are not “monster ancestry.” They are people who came through spiritual overexposure, metaphysical poisoning, signal corruption, hollow-light saturation, or direct contact with the wrong kind of reality and remained themselves enough to keep going. Their scars are not cosmetic. They are the visible proof that the inside and outside of a person do not always agree anymore.

In Bad Eden, they are common near broken shrines, corruption zones, deep wasteland anomalies, failed cult-sites, black-signal ruins, and places everyone else is smart enough to leave alone. They are invaluable in containment work, nightmare geography, and situations where the map has already started lying.

In the Harmonized Interior, they are rarer, heavily watched, often misunderstood, and quietly respected by the people who know what they’ve actually endured. Some become wardens, exorcists, diplomats for impossible things, or specialists in corruption response. Some simply try to live ordinary lives while humming ominously.

Rustlanders

Rustlanders are not symbolic in the same way Menhirkin are. They are one of the ancestries that exist partly because they are cool as hell and the world had room for them.

But even they are still a consequence.

Rustlanders are the people shaped by dead industry, toxic inheritance, salvage ecologies, and urban collapse so total it became a culture instead of a disaster. They are descendants of people who learned to breathe bad air, read junk like scripture, and turn the leftovers of empire into tomorrow’s breakfast.

In Bad Eden, they are everywhere there is scrap, ruin, black market oxygen, busted transit, or a half-dead industrial zone still pretending to be worth something. They are scavengers, mechanics, traders, salvage theologians, and expert witnesses in the case of “this should not still be functioning.”

In the Harmonized Interior, Rustlanders are often recruited into logistics, public works, repair guilds, reclamation corps, and the sort of civic maintenance jobs that decide whether a city remains “harmonized” or becomes “historically interesting.”

Sephirotic Scions

Sephirotic Scions are what happens when alignment is not merely moral but structural.

Some bloodlines, some births, some convergences, some sacred sites, some rituals, and some incomprehensible accidents produce people whose bodies and souls carry the architecture of the higher spheres more openly than most. They are not angels. They are not saints by default. They are people with too much metaphysical clarity in their bones.

In Bad Eden, this is dangerous. Scions attract attention, hope, resentment, prophecy, and gunfire. People project onto them immediately. Some become healers, lights in the dark, false messiahs, real messiahs, or cautionary tales.

In the Harmonized Interior, Scions tend to be folded into institutional life more readily. They serve in rites, diplomacy, alignment-work, education, Spark interpretation, and governance. They are still people, which means they remain capable of being wonderful, catastrophic, or both before lunch.

Stormborn Nomads

Stormborn come from migratory peoples shaped by weather severity, route knowledge, ritualized travel, and life on the edge of environmental violence. Where other ancestries are tied to ruin, stone, signal, or corruption, Stormborn are tied to motion through danger.

They are what the world makes when travel stops being movement and becomes a theology.

In Bad Eden, they run ash-waste routes, storm corridors, sink-mire crossings, high-risk caravan lines, and pilgrim roads no one sane would mark on a map. In the Harmonized Interior, they are couriers, guides, weather readers, and keepers of long-route memory.

Oldenborn

Oldenborn are not a single species so much as a category error with paperwork.

They are god-fragments, place-souls, ancestral memories, and mythic residues that found embodiment again after the Shattering. Earthbound, Ember-Touched, Lumenwrought, Sky-Threaded, Tideborne — these are not “subraces.” They are modes of remembered place made personal.

An Oldenborn does not descend from a biome.
An Oldenborn descends from a relationship.

Earthbound are stone, burden, patience, gravity, and endurance.
Ember-Touched are hearth, fire, renewal, hunger, and shelter.
Lumenwrought are glamour, memory, story, social gravity, and dream-light.
Sky-Threaded are wind, motion, change, altitude, and weather.
Tideborne are depth, emotion, oath, pressure, and memory in motion.

In Bad Eden, Oldenborn are revered, feared, hunted, misidentified, bargained with, and occasionally elected mayor for reasons no one can quite reconstruct. In the Harmonized Interior, they are better understood but no less strange. They often become ritualists, local patrons, guardians, public symbols, or walking constitutional crises.

Humans, Furrykin, Echo-Divers, and the Rest

Not every ancestry needs a cosmic dissertation.

Some are reawakened old-human lineages. Poor Homo sapiens had a rough century, and frankly the setting is showing them a little compassion by letting everybody else take a turn.

Some are beast-folk because beast-folk rule and the setting is better with them. Also, a furry convention at the time of the Shattering may have been involved, which is either apocryphal slander or the most Bad Eden thing anyone has ever said.

Some are weird because the world is weird, and a world this weird needs something that can survive anywhere. Just to hedge its bets.

The point is not that every ancestry emerged through the same mechanism.

The point is that after the Shattering, the world stopped making people for only one reason.

Now it makes them from memory.
From land.
From stress.
From function.
From symbolism.
From fallout.
From necessity.
From surprise.
From delight.
